episodes.title: The First Proof
episodes.intro: In the Alberta archive, a catalogue box holds a reproduction linked to William Caxton’s workshop. The archivist explains that Caxton is associated with bringing the press to England in the 1470s, although printing began much earlier in Asia. A modern exhibit label and a copied proof disagree. Which words belong to the old record, and which were added later?
episodes.problem: A copied exhibit label contains a spelling change and a missing capital that make its source unclear.
episodes.decision: Use language evidence to choose which transcription should remain attached to the reproduction.
episodes.consequence: The corrected label points to a second sheet filed under the wrong heading.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: Who copied the second sheet, and why did they change the heading?
episodes.reveal: The learner’s corrections show that the questionable line came from the modern exhibit label, not from the reproduced document. The archive record can now keep the two layers separate. A pencilled mark on the second sheet suggests that another person checked the copy, but the checker’s name is still missing.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: The National Archives associates William Caxton with England’s printing press and a 1476 printed item. The British Library notes that printing existed in China centuries before Europe. Invented: this archive box, exhibit label, proof, and pencilled clue. Uncertain: historians qualify some claims about who introduced a technology and when.

episodes.title: Marks in the Margin
episodes.intro: The second sheet resembles a printer’s working copy, but it is a fictional clue rather than a real archival item. Real collections about British printing preserve papers, letters, notes, drafts, and handwritten alterations. On this sheet, one margin note is only a fragment. Another is a complete direction. Identifying the complete thought will reveal where the copy travelled next.
episodes.problem: Fragments and complete directions have been mixed together in the margin.
episodes.decision: Identify the complete direction without pretending that the invented sheet is a historical source.
episodes.consequence: The direction names a port file, setting up the next chapter’s search.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: Was the letter in the port file sent to the person named on its cover?
episodes.reveal: Only the complete sentence gives an action that an archive worker could follow. It directs the investigator to compare the port register with a letter cover. The fragments remain useful as clues, but they cannot carry the full instruction alone. A different recipient name on the cover opens the next part of the case.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: British Library catalogue records about printing history include letters, memoranda, drafts, amendments, and handwritten copying. The National Archives preserves an item connected with Caxton’s early English printing. Invented: the margin directions, port file, and recipient puzzle. No sentence in this episode is presented as a quotation from a historical document.
